strengths: Significant practical contribution: 2-64× inference speedup (64ms vs 110-4140ms) with only 2-5 network evaluations, achieving a valuable speed-AUC trade-off for industrial applications
Eliminates hyperparameter tuning of perturbation timestep, making the approach more practical than reconstruction-based alternatives
Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies (Sections 5.3-5.4), evaluation on two benchmarks with both image-level and pixel-level metrics, and comparison with 8+ recent methods

Insightful analysis of reverse-scoring problem: identifies why log-likelihood degrades with more steps (Figure 2) and connects to OOD detection literature; proposes spatial norm-based scoring solution
Clear presentation and effective visualization: Figure 1 clearly contrasts reconstruction-based vs. reconstruction-free approaches; well-structured methodology
Sound technical implementation: Proper use of PF-ODE inversion, DDIM framework, and extension to feature-space diffusion models
weaknesses: Critical theoretical gap: Equation (16) shows log p_θ(x_0) requires a Jacobian term, but the paper dismisses this without rigorous justification. Citing normalizing flow practices is insufficient; the impact of this approximation on diffusion-based detection is not properly analyzed

Ad-hoc anomaly scoring function: The spatial norm difference (Eq. 17) lacks principled theoretical justification. Authors acknowledge it's a workaround for reverse-scoring and that 'rigorous theoretical interpretation remains open,' suggesting the core metric is fundamentally problematic

Severe pixel-level localization weakness: Pixel-level AUC often 5-25% lower than competitors (93.7% vs 98.1% for GLAD). Catastrophic failures on specific categories (metal nut: 71.9% vs 98.8%, screw: 95.4% vs 99.3%) limit real-world defect localization applicability. No analysis provided

Inconsistent cross-dataset performance: 18.2% image-level AUC drop on VisA (97.3% → 79.1%) compared to MVTecAD with no explanation. 'Ours*' requires tuning S on VisA, contradicting the no-tuning claim

Unexplained performance instability: Table 4 shows catastrophic NLL-based degradation with more steps (96.9% at S=3 → 59.5% at S=1000). While spatial norm stabilizes this, relying on a heuristic workaround raises robustness concerns

Limited technical novelty: PF-ODE inversion directly from Song et al. (DDIM), feature-space diffusion from Rombach et al. (LDM). Main contribution is applying existing techniques to anomaly detection; technical innovation is incremental

Incomplete experimental analysis: (1) No comparison with fast non-diffusion baselines (memory-based, reconstruction-based methods); (2) Reconstruction baseline in Table 4 appears suboptimal; (3) No failure case visualization or analysis; (4) Threshold selection process (τ) not discussed despite being crucial for deployment

Missing practical details: Algorithm 1's 'Normalize' operation vaguely defined; training stability of feature-space diffusion not analyzed; VisA results suggest S must be dataset-tuned, contradicting no-hyperparameter-tuning claim

strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing genuine limitations: eliminates need for reconstruction by inferring latent variables via PF-ODE inversion, removing both expensive forward passes and perturbation timestep tuning
Substantial computational efficiency gain: achieves 2-5 NFE with ~64ms latency versus 110-4140ms for baselines, representing 2-64× speedup with practical value for real-time applications

Useful empirical analysis: systematic comparison between reconstruction and inversion approaches (Section 5.3) and investigation of reverse-scoring phenomenon with clear visualizations (Figure 2, Table 4)
Competitive image-level performance on MVTecAD: 97.3% (Ours) and 99.1% (Ours*) AUC demonstrates feasibility of the approach for main benchmark
Feature-space diffusion design leverages pre-trained backbone representations effectively
weaknesses: Significant undisclosed accuracy degradation on pixel-level and VisA: pixel-level AUC drops from 94.8-98.1% (baselines) to 93.7% (Ours) with severe category-specific failures (metal_nut: 71.9% vs 97-100%, grid: 95.3% vs 99.6%); VisA collapses to 79.1% vs 98.9% baseline—a 20% gap that contradicts claims of 'competitive performance'

Fundamental flaw in anomaly scoring: direct NLL approach admittedly 'fails to capture small anomalies' (Section 4.4); proposed spatial norm scoring (Eq. 17) appears ad-hoc and unprincipled, combining heuristics (channel norms, max-min differences) without theoretical justification or systematic design ablation

Reverse-scoring problem reveals core design failure: Table 4 shows NLL scoring collapses from 96.9% to 59.5% as S increases, while ad-hoc spatial scoring maintains ~96.5%—indicating the latent density does not genuinely capture typicality as theorized; the fix bypasses rather than resolves the fundamental issue

Critical theoretical assumptions inadequately justified: (1) Jacobian term omission (Eq. 16) posed as research question but never rigorously evaluated empirically; (2) Euler approximation validity with S=2-5 lacks convergence analysis or error bounds; (3) Gaussian assumption for x_T with few steps not validated despite massive gap between T=1000 training and S=2-5 testing

Limited evaluation scope with no cross-dataset generalization: only two datasets (MVTecAD, VisA); VisA results are particularly weak; no evaluation on other benchmarks despite mentioning medical imaging/video in conclusion; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned, missing implementation details (exact backbone layer, learning rate schedule details), insufficient information for independent reproduction

Presentation issues: Figure 1 duplicated, Section 3.4 verbatim repetition of earlier content, Algorithm 1 lacks clear justification for specific anomaly score formula, ambiguity about whether feature extraction time is included in latency measurements

Misleading framing: 'Ours*' involves tuning S ∈ {2,3,4,5} contradicting 'no hyperparameter tuning' claim; title 'reconstruction-free' is somewhat misleading as method still requires training full diffusion model; 'state-of-the-art speed-AUC trade-off' overstated given VisA performance

strengths: Novel inversion-based approach that replaces reconstruction with direct latent evaluation via PF-ODE trajectory, with clear motivation addressing limitations of noise-strength tuning and multiple forward passes
Significant practical speed improvement of 2-64× (achieving 64ms/15 FPS vs 675-4140ms) while maintaining competitive accuracy on MVTecAD (99.1% average AUC with Ours*)
Removes hyperparameter tuning requirement for perturbation timestep while avoiding synthetic anomalies, improving practical applicability
Comprehensive empirical evaluation including ablation studies (Section 5.3-5.4) that validate design choices and reveal the reverse-scoring phenomenon with thoughtful analysis
Practical feature-space diffusion design that leverages pre-trained backbones effectively in the inversion setting
Clear presentation with effective visual comparison (Figure 1) and reproducible algorithm (Algorithm 1)
weaknesses: Significant generalization concern: 20% performance drop on VisA dataset without tuning (79.1% vs 98.9% Ours*), with no root cause analysis or solution provided despite claims about robustness

Theoretical gaps in key design choices: (1) Jacobian correction term omitted in Eq. 16 with limited rigorous justification; (2) Why 2-5 step inversion remains effective vs 1000 training steps lacks theoretical explanation; (3) Reverse-scoring phenomenon identified but not mechanistically explained
Spatial norm-based anomaly scoring (Eq. 17) lacks principled justification and appears ad-hoc; the paper acknowledges theoretical interpretation remains an open question
Notably weaker pixel-level localization accuracy (94.8% vs 98.8-98.1% for competitors), representing a 4-5% trade-off not thoroughly discussed or analyzed
Limited generalization evidence: only evaluated on industrial inspection datasets (MVTecAD, VisA); no experiments on medical imaging or diverse anomaly types despite mentioning as future work
Inconsistent tuning claims: while claiming to avoid timestep tuning, Ours* tunes S ∈ {2,3,4,5} per category, which is still hyperparameter selection
Category-specific performance failures unexplained (metal nut 93.6%, screw 88.7%, transistor 94.4% vs 99-100% for competitors) with no error analysis or failure case visualization
Step selection strategy (τ₃ = [333, 666, 999]) appears arbitrary with no ablation on alternative sampling strategies (logarithmic, learned, etc.)

strengths: Novel and well-motivated inversion-based paradigm addressing genuine limitations of existing diffusion-based AD methods in computational efficiency
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three major benchmarks (MVTecAD, VisA, MPDD) with detailed per-category results and extensive ablation studies
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance (96.1-99.1% AU-ROC) with significant efficiency gains (~88 FPS)
Rigorous methodology with clear mathematical formulation (Eqs. 1-8), pseudo-code algorithm, and detailed reproducibility information including hyperparameters and implementation details
Demonstrates method generalizability via successful incorporation into other diffusion-based AD approaches (Table 5) and effective pixel-level anomaly localization visualizations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: PF-ODE inversion is not new; primary contribution is applying existing technique to AD with a relatively straightforward scoring scheme lacking rigorous justification
Weak theoretical foundation: No rigorous analysis of why anomalies deviate in learned latent distributions or why latent-space detection outperforms RGB-space; assumptions stated but not validated

Concerning backbone dependency: Table 6 shows dramatic performance variation (87.1%-99.0%) suggesting success depends more on feature extractor quality than on the proposed mechanism; insufficient explanation of why pre-training backbone matters in diffusion latent space

Limited generalization evidence: Primarily evaluated on visually similar industrial datasets; medical imaging results (BMAD: 87.4%) significantly weaker, suggesting domain-specific performance without clear understanding of generalizability

Hyperparameter sensitivity without guidance: Method sensitive to diffusion steps S and subset selection τ_S (Table 4) with limited guidance for new datasets; efficiency and accuracy trade-offs not thoroughly analyzed
Insufficient analysis of when and why method fails: No failure case analysis, no statistical significance testing, marginal improvements sometimes (96.3% vs 96.1%), incomplete ablations

Efficiency claims need stronger justification: 5× speedup mentioned but not rigorously analyzed; comparison with methods using 1000 steps seems unfair; efficiency gain primarily from skipping reconstruction is somewhat obvious

Presentation clarity issues: Notation could be clearer; derivation bridge from theory to algorithm not explicit; some critical design choices lack justification; important details relegated to appendix

strengths: Addresses genuine limitations of reconstruction-based AD methods with a conceptually different approach (latent-space inversion via PF-ODE)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three major benchmarks (MVTecAD, VisA, MPDD) with detailed ablations and supplementary analyses
Achieves practical efficiency improvements (~88.1 FPS) and enables plug-and-play integration with existing diffusion-based AD methods
Strong empirical results with competitive AU-ROC scores across multiple datasets and object categories
Well-documented implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—core contribution is primarily replacing reconstruction with latent-space inversion using existing PF-ODE machinery; most components (DDIM, backbones, Gaussian anomaly detection) are borrowed from prior work

Weak theoretical justification for why latent-space anomaly detection should be fundamentally superior; lacks rigorous analysis of learned latent distribution properties and their relationship to anomaly detection

Marginal empirical improvements over recent baselines (Table 2-3 show differences of 1-2 AU-ROC points); without error bars or significance testing, unclear if improvements are statistically meaningful
Misleading efficiency claims—method still requires T forward diffusion passes; 'reconstruction-free' terminology obscures that forward encoding remains necessary

Generalization concerns evidenced by significantly lower BMAD performance (77.5% vs 99%+ on MVTecAD); limited domain diversity with all benchmarks focused on industrial/object defects; no cross-dataset evaluation

Incomplete analysis of why latent space is fundamentally better (no comparison with alternative approaches); missing ablations on noise schedule justification; insufficient investigation of failure cases or anomaly types where method underperforms
Questionable fairness of comparisons—Table 1 shows different methods use different scoring schemes; missing analysis of simpler alternatives (e.g., L2 in reconstruction space)
Lack of statistical rigor—no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests reported despite marginal improvements

strengths: Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance across three major benchmarks (MVTecAD, VisA, MPDD) with comprehensive evaluation at both image and pixel levels
Significant efficiency gains (88.1 FPS) demonstrating effective inference with only 3 diffusion steps while maintaining high accuracy, providing practical value for real-time applications
Novel inversion-based paradigm shift from reconstruction-based methods with clean conceptual framework and clear motivation supported by effective visualizations
Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablations (Tables 4-7), generalizability studies (Table 5), and consistent per-category performance across diverse defect types
Technically sound mathematical formulation with proper derivations of continuous and discrete-time formulations connecting to Probability Flow ODE theory
Demonstrated applicability as a plug-and-play module that can enhance other diffusion-based AD methods without requiring retraining
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily a repositioning of established techniques (diffusion models, PF-ODE, Euler methods) rather than introducing new algorithmic innovations

Claims of being 'reconstruction-free' are imprecise; the method avoids explicit pixel-space reconstruction but still leverages inherent reconstruction in diffusion models—terminology could be more precise
Incomplete comparative analysis with several N/A entries in comparisons (Table 2), potential fairness issues in FPS comparisons across implementations, and lack of error bars or confidence intervals

Insufficient analysis of method limitations including no systematic failure case study, minimal theoretical justification for why latent inversion outperforms reconstruction-based approaches beyond empirics, and limited exploration of anomaly types where method struggles
Experimental scope primarily limited to industrial defect detection; generalization to other AD domains (medical, surveillance) and cross-domain robustness not thoroughly evaluated

Missing design justifications: hyperparameter choices (Table 9) lack thorough motivation, backbone architecture impact (EfficientNet-B4) unexplored, and no code availability mentioned, limiting reproducibility
